title: Tokens-per-Parameter Coverage Is Critical for Robust LLM Scaling Law Extrapolation
claim: Fits from a single collinear design extrapolate poorly off the training ray, while designs with diverse ratios generalize far better.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right; 3D surface, error-bar plot, curve plot, shared CO/NC colors
description: Three side-by-side plots compare collinear (CO) and non-collinear (NC) fits of a Kaplan scaling law on RedPajama. Panel (a) is a 3D loss surface over N and D. A blue CO surface and a red NC surface sit above black holdout points, with green and black residual bars. The legend gives R² of 0.511 for CO and 0.906 for NC. Panel (b) plots holdout R² against coverage fraction. The red NC curve sits near 0.8 to 0.9 with small error bars. The blue CO curve sits near 0.4 to 0.5 with large error bars. Panel (c) shows induced isoFLOP curves of loss versus N on a log axis. Dashed CO curves and solid NC curves are coloured purple to yellow by compute. Holdout points and residual bars sit on the curves, and a long legend lists the compute values. The eye goes first to the 3D surface, then to the gap between the red and blue curves in (b).
caption: Kaplan law on RedPajama, first epoch (seed-0 CO holdout R2 =0.51, NC R2 =0.91; CO blue, NC red in (a)-(b), dashed and solid in (c)). (a), (c): seed 0, whose NC (Nc, Dc) is a start draw (Appendix E.7); (b): mean over 30 seeds with 5th-95th percentile bars, from two rays on, as CO’s one-ray mean is R2 = −1.35. (a) Fitted surface ˆL(N, D; θ) with holdout points and residual bars. (c) Induced isoFLOP curves (Definition 4), one per kept holdout point (highest D per unique N), with residual bars at each Ni; curves and markers share a colormap ordered by Ci = 6NiDi.
abstract: Neural scaling laws approximate a language model's loss as a power-law function of parameter count $N$ and token count $D$. Following Chinchilla-style compute-optimal training, many studies fit scaling laws from runs at one or a few fixed tokens-per-parameter (TPP) ratios $k$, with $D = kN$. We show that this collinear design, combined with the empirically common near-equality of the exponents governing $N$ and $D$, induces an inherent ill-conditioning in the Gauss-Newton least-squares problem: the condition number of the design grows as the inverse square of the gap between the $N$- and $D$-exponents. The scale coefficients become practically unidentifiable, with confidence intervals inflating by orders of magnitude, yielding a "sloppy" model whose extrapolations degrade sharply off the training ray. We prove this for four scaling-law formalisms and derive a closed-form TPP-diversity threshold that characterizes well-conditioned estimation to leading order. Empirically, in controlled experiments with 5M-77M-parameter models, non-collinear designs outperform collinear ones on held-out data with a 97.3% win rate across four laws and five corpora, and 98.7% in bfloat16. We further show the degeneracy is rooted in Jacobian geometry and is not an artifact of the loss function: any smooth objective whose Gauss-Newton weights are bounded above and away from zero inherits the same ill-conditioning.
